'''''Solanum rostratum'''''  is a species of nightshade (genus ''[[Solanum]]'') that is native to the [[United States]] and northern and central [[Mexico]].<ref name="GRIN"/> [[Common name]]s include '''buffalobur nightshade''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SORO|taxon=Solanum rostratum|accessdate=17 November 2015}}</ref> '''buffalo-bur''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> '''spiny nightshade''', '''Colorado bur''', '''Kansas thistle''', '''bad woman''', '''Mexican thistle''', and '''Texas thistle'''.

It is an [[Annual plant|annual]], self-compatible [[Herbaceous plant|herb]] that forms a [[tumbleweed]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Some Weeds of Iowa |author=Louis Hermann Pammel |publisher=Experiment Station, Iowa State College of Agriculture and the Mechanic Arts |year=1903 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=croUAAAAYAAJ}} page 477</ref> Individual plants reach {{convert|1|-|1.5|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, have once or twice pinnatified leaves (see image of leaf), and abundant spines on the stems and leaves. It produces yellow [[flower]]s with pentagonal [[Corolla (flower)|corollas]] {{convert|2|-|3.5|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter and weakly bilaterally symmetric (see flower-closeup image).<ref>{{cite journal |first=M.D. |last=Whalen |title=Taxonomy of Solanum section Androceras |journal=Gentes Herbarum |volume=11 |issue=6 |pages=359–426 |year=1979}}</ref> In its native range ''S. rostratum'' is pollinated by medium- to large-sized [[bee]]s including [[bumblebee]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |first=K.A.W. |last=Bowers |title=The pollination ecology of ''Solanum rostratum'' (Solanaceae) |journal=American Journal of Botany |volume=62 |issue=6 |pages=633–8 |year=1975 |jstor=2441943 |doi=10.1002/j.1537-2197.1975.tb14094.x}}</ref>

''Solanum rostratum'' flowers exhibit [[wikt:heteranthery|heteranthery]], i.e. they bear two sets of [[anther]]s of unequal size, possibly distinct colouration, and divergence in ecological function between pollination and feeding.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vallejo-Marin |first1=M. |last2=Manson |first2=J.S. |last3=Thomson |first3=J.D. |last4=Barrett |first4=S.C.H. |title=Division of labour within flowers: Heteranthery, a floral strategy to reconcile contrasting pollen fates |journal=Journal of Evolutionary Biology |volume=22 |issue=4 |pages=828–839 |year=2009 |doi=10.1111/j.1420-9101.2009.01693.x |pmid=19320798 |hdl=1893/942 |s2cid=36383835 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> The [[fruit]], a [[Berry (botany)|berry]], is enclosed by a prickly [[Sepal|calyx]]. The [[seed]]s are released when the berries dry and [[Dehiscence (botany)|dehisce]] (split apart) while still attached to the plant.

This species represents one of the later scientific interests of famed biologist [[Charles Darwin]], who just over a week prior to his death had ordered seeds from a colleague in America, so as to investigate their [[wikt:heteranthery|heteranthery]], a topic he was interested in.<ref>{{cite book |first=S.L. |last=Buchmann |chapter=Buzz pollination in angiosperms |editor-last=Jones |editor-first=C.E. |editor2-last=Little |editor2-first=R.J. |title=Handbook of experimental pollination biology |publisher=Van Nostrand Reinhold |year=1983 |isbn=0442246765 |pages=73–113}}</ref>

''Solanum rostratum'' is the ancestral host plant of the [[Colorado potato beetle]], ''Leptinotarsa decemlineata'', but this pest adopted the [[potato]], ''Solanum tuberosum'' as a new (and more succulent) host, a fact first reported in eastern Nebraska in 1859. It then expanded its range rapidly eastward on potato crops in the next two decades.<ref>Riley CV. 1876. ''Potato Pests''. New York, Orange Judd Co., 108pp.</ref>  Can be invasive.
